content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has estimated that over one billion people currently require one or more assistive products, with the majority being older adults and individuals with disabilities. As populations age and the prevalence of noncommunicable diseases rises, the number of people needing assistive products is projected to exceed two billion by 2050. However, only one in ten individuals in need currently has access to assistive technology. This lack of access often leads to social exclusion, poverty, and isolation, exacerbating the impact of disease and disability on individuals, their families, and society as a whole. To address this significant gap between the need for and provision of assistive technology, WHO launched the Global Cooperation on Assistive Health Technology (GATE) initiative. This initiative prioritizes research and innovation as key focus areas. To advance these efforts, WHO convened a core group of experts to identify strategic research priorities for the GATE initiative. This culminated in a GATE Research Group meeting held in Budapest in September 2015, which included experts from organizations such as the Association for the Advancement of Assistive Technology in Europe (AAATE), the Rehabilitation Engineering and Assistive Technology Society of North America (RESNA), Zuyd University of Applied Sciences, and Trinity College Dublin. The GATE Research Group identified five global priority research areas essential for improving access to high-quality, affordable assistive technology: 1. Effects, Costs, and Economic Impact of Assistive Technology: There is limited evidence on the impact of assistive technology on quality of life, as well as its associated costs and societal benefits, such as reduced disability prevalence. Research is needed to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of assistive technology and its broader economic implications. 2. Policies, Systems, Service Provision Models, and Best Practices: Many countries lack effective policies and systems for assistive technology provision. Research is required to identify the most effective and efficient approaches, develop quality standards, and disseminate best practices to improve service delivery. 3. High-Quality and Affordable Assistive Technology: While high-income countries often focus on advanced, high-cost solutions, there is a critical need for robust, affordable, and high-quality assistive products in lowand middle-income countries. Research should prioritize the development of cost-effective solutions to bridge the assistive technology divide. 4. Human Resources for the Assistive Technology Sector: Professionals in healthcare, rehabilitation, education, and social work require specialized knowledge to provide quality advice and services related to assistive technology. Research is needed to establish standardized training programs and curricula to build capacity in this sector. 5. Standards and Methodologies for Assessing Assistive Technology Needs and Unmet Needs: Tools and methodologies are required to accurately assess the demand for assistive technology at national, regional, and local levels. This includes collecting reliable data on disability prevalence and mapping coverage and user satisfaction rates. The GATE initiative emphasizes two guiding principles for all research efforts: the involvement of end-users in all aspects of research, policy development, and service provision, and the adoption of an environmental approach to functioning rather than a purely medical model. The global priority research agenda developed through this process serves as a call to action for researchers, governments, donor agencies, user groups, and other stakeholders to initiate and support research activities that address the unmet needs for assistive technology worldwide. By closing this gap, the initiative seeks to enhance the quality of life, productivity, and human rights of individuals in need of assistive technology.
